title: Dynamic Topology Quantum Information Encoding (DTQE)
abstract: The development of efficient quantum information encoding methods is a crucial area of research in quantum information theory. Traditional approaches often rely on static quantum states, limiting their potential for enhanced storage and transmission efficiency. This paper introduces Dynamic Topology Quantum Information Encoding (DTQE), a novel approach that leverages the topological properties of quantum states to encode information. We propose a method where the inherent topology of a quantum state is dynamically encoded, providing a fundamentally different approach to quantum information processing. This novel technique demonstrates improved storage efficiency and enhanced transmission rates compared to existing encoding schemes. The core of this work lies in the use of topological transformations to map quantum states into a more structured and robust representation, ultimately leading to improved information fidelity and scalability.

title: Dynamic Quantum Control via Feedback Learning Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to dynamic quantum control utilizing feedback learning algorithms. The core idea is to develop a system capable of real-time adjustment of control parameters based on feedback information obtained from the quantum system itself. This approach addresses the inherent challenges in precisely controlling quantum systems, which are often highly sensitive to environmental noise and difficult to model accurately. The proposed framework leverages the principles of quantum control and feedback learning to achieve optimal control performance. The system architecture incorporates a closed-loop control mechanism where the system's output is continuously monitored, and the control parameters are adjusted accordingly. Mathematical formulations detailing the control process, feedback mechanisms, and optimization strategies are provided. This work contributes to advancements in quantum control by offering a robust and adaptable method for manipulating quantum states, with potential applications in quantum computing, quantum sensing, and quantum communication. The algorithm is designed to minimize the influence of external disturbances and maximize the accuracy of state preparation and manipulation. The presented approach provides a pathway towards more reliable and efficient quantum control strategies.

title: Scalability Analysis of Distributed Kolmogorov-Arnold Network Training on High-Performance Computing Systems
abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) replace the fixed activation functions and linear weights of Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) with learnable univariate functions on network edges, offering improved interpretability and, in some settings, competitive parameter efficiency. While the approximation properties of KANs have received considerable attention, their behavior under distributed, multi-GPU training has not been systematically characterized. This paper presents an empirical scalability study of data-parallel KAN training on multi-node, multi-GPU high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure, evaluated along four dimensions: strong scaling, weak scaling, communication overhead, and model-size scaling. Experiments were conducted on the FinisTerrae III supercomputer using up to 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs across 4 nodes with PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel (DDP). KAN training reaches 74.7% parallel efficiency at 8 GPUs with a 5.97x speedup, consistent with conventional deep learning workloads. Weak scaling shows an initial single-to-multi-GPU throughput drop followed by strong stability. Communication overhead follows a non-monotonic pattern (1.3%-6.1%), driven primarily by All-Reduce algorithm selection and inter-node latency rather than KAN's edge-wise gradient structure. The parameter-to-memory ratio improves with model size even as training time scales unfavorably. These results indicate that operator-level and data-parallel optimizations for KAN are complementary. We provide deployment guidelines for GPU topology and model-size selection, and discuss the limitations of a synthetic-regression evaluation.

title: CIT-CAD: Constraint Intent Tree-based CAD Code Generation and Verification
abstract: Natural-language Computer-Aided Design (CAD) code generation aims to turn design intent into executable and editable parametric programs. Large language models (LLMs) make this goal increasingly practical, but useful systems must preserve the construction process behind the rendered geometry. Existing benchmarks and methods mostly focus on how closely the generated CAD model matches the reference geometry, often using metrics such as Intersection over Union (IoU). Such metrics can miss errors in part decomposition, construction hierarchy, Boolean operations, sketch structure, and geometric relations. This gap calls for a representation that makes design intent explicit and lets a system check generated code against that intent. We propose CIT-CAD, a framework that infers a Constraint Intent Tree (CIT) from the input description to represent the intended entities, hierarchy, operations, and relations. The tree has two roles: it guides CAD code generation and defines expected constraints for verification. The framework extracts actual constraints from the generated program, compares them with the expected constraints, and uses mismatches to localize and repair design violations. Experiments show that the framework improves CAD generation performance, with larger gains on more complex multi-entity designs. By turning design intent into an explicit and checkable object, this work is the first attempt to move text-to-CAD generation beyond rendered-geometry matching toward construction-aware synthesis, verification, and repair.

title: The Measurement Gap
abstract: This essay argues that the AI capability question posed by "Situational Awareness" (Aschenbrenner, 2024) has, on its own terms, mostly been answered, and has turned into a measurement question that no current benchmark can settle. In the first week of September 2026, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra scored 62.7% and 99.9% on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark with the same underlying weights, depending only on which evaluation harness was used. This essay treats that result as the central data point. Part I re-grades the 2024 "Situational Awareness" predictions against September 2026 evidence. Part II decomposes the Astra result, defines a "harness ratio" (H) for separating model capability from scaffold-provided capability, and fits a half-life to the ARC-AGI benchmark series (roughly 61 months, 12 months, then 6 months across three generations). Part III proposes DRIFT (Dynamic Rule Inference and Fast Transfer), a benchmark that measures adaptation to unannounced mid-episode rule changes as a rate against a human baseline, rather than a static pass/fail score. A minimum-viable prototype design is included. Part IV states nine dated, falsifiable predictions through September 2028. Written with Claude Fable 5.1 as a research and drafting collaborator; the argument, editing, and any errors are the author's own. All figures were checked against primary sources as of September 7, 2026. Companion site with rendered mathematics: https://measurementgap.com

title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithms for Large-Scale Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum-inspired algorithms for tackling large-scale optimization problems. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with the computational complexity of problems involving numerous variables and constraints. Quantum mechanics, particularly concepts like superposition and entanglement, offers a radically different approach to problem-solving. This work investigates how these concepts can be translated into algorithmic designs, aiming to improve the efficiency and speed of optimization processes. We propose a framework for developing algorithms that mimic quantum phenomena, focusing on techniques that enable exploration of the solution space in a more parallel and potentially faster manner. The core of this approach lies in leveraging mathematical structures derived from quantum mechanics to guide search strategies. We outline key algorithmic ideas, emphasizing the potential for improved convergence rates and scalability. The presented concepts represent a novel application of quantum-inspired ideas to the field of optimization, offering a promising avenue for addressing complex real-world problems.

title: Quantum Probability Field Theory: Adaptive Parameterization
abstract: Quantum probability field theory (QPF) offers a fundamentally different approach to quantum computing and information processing compared to traditional quantum algorithms. This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework, the adaptive parameterization of quantum probability fields, leveraging quantum entanglement and measurement to dynamically adjust quantum states. We argue that this approach represents a significant step toward achieving more precise quantum state descriptions and calculations, potentially overcoming limitations imposed by current computational paradigms. The core mechanism involves designing a parameterization that responds to quantum measurements, effectively fine-tuning the quantum state through a process of continuous adjustment. This dynamic adjustment aims to enhance the accuracy and robustness of quantum computations, representing a new direction in quantum information theory.

title: Causal Bayesian Networks with Temporal Dynamics
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to representing causal relationships using Causal Bayesian Networks with Temporal Dynamics. Traditional Bayesian Networks, while effective in depicting static causal dependencies, often fail to capture the intricate dynamics of systems influenced by time, feedback loops, and evolving causal links. This work proposes an extension to Bayesian networks that incorporates temporal modeling, allowing for the simulation of system behavior under various interventions and the prediction of future states. The core claim is that representing causal relationships with temporal dynamics significantly enhances the modeling capabilities of Bayesian networks. The key mechanism involves extending the network structure to account for changes in causal dependencies over time. This approach addresses the limitations of static Bayesian networks and provides a more realistic and accurate representation of complex, dynamic systems. The resulting models are capable of predicting system behavior under different interventions, offering significant advantages in fields such as epidemiology, economics, and engineering. The presented framework is designed for flexibility and scalability, accommodating varying degrees of temporal complexity. The paper outlines the core concepts, provides a formal representation of the model, and discusses potential applications.

title: Information-Theoretic Regularization of Neural Networks
abstract: Deep neural networks, despite their impressive performance, often suffer from an inherent information bottleneck. Standard regularization techniques, such as L1/L2 regularization and dropout, primarily address overfitting by reducing the model's complexity, but they fail to directly tackle the fundamental issue of information loss during the compression of high-dimensional input into lower-dimensional representations. This paper proposes a novel regularization framework that directly addresses this problem by incorporating information-theoretic measures – specifically mutual information and entropy – into the training process. The core idea is to minimize the loss of information during the encoding of the input into the network's internal representations. We introduce a differentiable information-theoretic loss function that can be directly integrated into the network's objective function. This approach provides a principled way to control information flow and, consequently, improve the generalization ability of neural networks. We demonstrate, conceptually, the potential of this method and outline a pathway for future research.

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Pareto Dominance-Based Exploration
abstract: Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) presents significant challenges due to the difficulty in balancing multiple, often conflicting, objectives. Traditional exploration methods often fail to adequately explore the complex multi-objective action space, leading to suboptimal solutions. This paper proposes a novel exploration strategy for MORL that leverages Pareto dominance to efficiently navigate this space. The core idea is to guide the agent's exploration towards regions where it can achieve better trade-offs between objectives, as defined by Pareto dominance. We formulate the exploration process using a dominance-based ranking of solutions, allowing the agent to systematically identify and target superior solutions. This approach aims to mitigate the "curse of dimensionality" inherent in MORL and improve the convergence towards optimal multi-objective policies. The theoretical framework outlines the key concepts and provides a basis for further research in this area.

title: Causal Machine Learning: A Physics-Based Approach
abstract: Traditional machine learning models often struggle with issues of bias, poor generalization, and a lack of interpretability. These limitations stem from their reliance on purely correlational relationships between variables, without explicitly accounting for underlying causal mechanisms. This paper proposes a novel approach to machine learning – Causal Machine Learning (CML) – that leverages the principles of physics-based causal inference. The core idea is to build machine learning models rooted in causal graphs, enabling the identification and utilization of true causal relationships between variables. This framework allows for more robust model training, improved generalization performance, and enhanced interpretability. We introduce a methodology for constructing causal models from observational data, focusing on techniques for identifying and quantifying causal effects. The resulting models are then used for prediction and, crucially, for understanding the underlying mechanisms driving the observed data. This approach addresses key challenges in traditional machine learning by incorporating a fundamentally more realistic representation of the world – one governed by causal laws. We demonstrate the potential benefits of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline future research directions.

title: Fractal-Based Representation of Neural Network Architectures
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to analyzing and designing neural network architectures by leveraging the principles of fractal geometry. The core idea is to represent the intricate connections and layered structure of a neural network as a fractal. This representation allows for a more intuitive understanding of architectural complexity, facilitates the identification of critical bottlenecks, and potentially guides the design of more efficient and robust networks. We outline a mapping methodology and explore the potential benefits of this fractal-based approach, focusing on the inherent self-similarity properties of fractals. The resulting fractal structure provides a powerful tool for visualizing and quantifying network architecture, offering a new perspective on optimization and design. Further research will explore the application of fractal analysis to various neural network designs and its impact on performance metrics.

title: Self-Organizing Constraint System for Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-organizing constraint system for evolutionary algorithms designed to enhance solution fitness through dynamic constraint adjustment. Traditional evolutionary algorithms often rely on predefined constraints, which can limit the search space and hinder optimization. Our approach dynamically modifies constraints based on the algorithm's progress, allowing the system to intelligently guide the search towards more promising solutions. We detail the core mechanism, including a fitness monitoring loop and constraint modification strategy. The benefits of this system, including improved convergence speed and solution quality, are explored, with a focused discussion on its practical implications. Keywords: Evolutionary Algorithms, Constraint System, Dynamic Adjustment, Fitness Optimization, Self-Organization.

title: Neural Symbolic Hybrid Systems for Robust Reasoning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to artificial intelligence by integrating neural networks and symbolic reasoning, resulting in Neural Symbolic Hybrid Systems. The core claim is that combining the strengths of both paradigms—the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks and the logical inference capabilities of symbolic systems—yields more robust and explainable AI systems. The proposed system utilizes neural networks for perceptual tasks, such as feature extraction and initial data interpretation, while employing symbolic reasoning engines for higher-level logical inference, decision-making, and knowledge representation. The system architecture is designed to facilitate seamless interaction between these two components. Specifically, the neural network outputs are translated into symbolic representations, which are then processed by the reasoning engine. Conversely, the symbolic reasoning engine's conclusions are fed back into the neural network for refinement and improved accuracy. This hybrid approach addresses limitations inherent in purely neural or purely symbolic systems. Neural networks alone can lack explainability and robustness against noisy or incomplete data, while symbolic systems often struggle with complex, real-world scenarios requiring flexible pattern recognition. This paper outlines the core mechanisms, architecture, and potential benefits of such a system, highlighting its capacity for robust reasoning and enhanced interpretability. The system is envisioned as a significant step towards developing more reliable and trustworthy AI solutions.

title: Dynamic Programming for Quantum Circuit Optimization with Uncertainty
abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is a crucial step in realizing the full potential of quantum computing. However, the inherent uncertainty in quantum gate fidelities and measurement outcomes presents a significant challenge. Traditional optimization methods often fail to adequately address this probabilistic nature. This paper proposes a novel dynamic programming approach for quantum circuit optimization that explicitly incorporates uncertainty. The algorithm constructs an optimal circuit path by minimizing the expected cost, which accounts for the potential error associated with each gate operation and measurement. This framework allows for a more accurate and robust optimization process, leading to circuits with reduced error and improved performance. The core claim is that dynamic programming can be effectively applied to quantum circuit optimization, acknowledging and utilizing the probabilistic elements. The key mechanism involves a structured, iterative process to evaluate and select the best circuit paths based on a quantified uncertainty model. This approach avoids the limitations of purely deterministic optimization techniques when dealing with quantum systems.

title: Lost in Explanation: Can Cognitive Forcing Counteract Over-Reliance Across Sentiment, Irony, and Sarcasm?
abstract: While explanations in AI-assisted decision-making are intended to build trust, they can also cause users to over-rely on incorrect predictions. We investigate whether this effect changes depending on how subjective the underlying NLP task is. We present participants with sentences varying in subjectivity—sentiment, irony, and sarcasm—and ask them to judge the intended meaning. Each participant completes all three explanation conditions—no explanation (Control), a standard explanation (Standard NLE), or an explanation that also points to a plausible alternative reading (Cognitive Forcing NLE)—with condition order counterbalanced across participants. Participants first give an initial judgment, then see the model's prediction accompanied by the explanation for that condition (if any), and finally give a final decision. We test whether over-reliance increases with task subjectivity (H1), whether a standard explanation increases over-reliance relative to no explanation (H2), whether an explanation surfacing an alternative reading reduces over-reliance relative to a standard explanation (H3), and, exploratively, whether this reduction is larger for more subjective tasks (H4). This study is conducted as part of the Natural Language Processing 2 course at the University of Regensburg.

title: <!--Does This Affect the Interpretation of What Follows?-->
abstract: By defining the content of formal ontologies, we can determine, for the ontology, the truth value of any statement that refers to, or does not refer to, that content. This is not possible for all XML documents. The main reason for this is that, unlike ontologies, XML does not inherently embrace any principle for handling known and unknown information as a metalanguage. This allows the application of different principles to the same XML document, which generate different interpretations of it, thereby undermining the communication between people and software applications that XML, like ontologies, is supposed to support. In this paper, I propose a solution for XML documents to come close to achieving the same result as ontologies: including comments that contain principles for handling known and unknown information. In demonstrating that this solution works only under very specific circumstances, I also focus on the communication that ontologies and XML documents are intended to support, highlighting the different roles they assign to the subjects engaging with their content: spectators and interpreters, respectively. More specifically, I argue that the fact that the subjects (whether people or software applications) have ultimate authority over the interpretation of XML documents renders the documents hermeneutically unstable – an instability that even the inclusion of a comment specifying a principle for handling known and unknown information shifts rather than definitively resolves.

title: Dimensionality Reduction Networks and Autoencoders
abstract: Autoencoders (AEs) have become indispensable tools for a wide range of DIP tasks, including feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and noise filtering. This chapter provides a comprehensive introduction to various linear and nonlinear AEs. We begin by presenting a linear AE network that implements Principal Component Analysis (PCA) using a modified Hebbian learning rule, alongside an efficient recursive least squares (RLS)-based unsupervised learning approach for sequential PCA extraction. As for nonlinear approaches, we introduce two separate lines of approaches, including a manifold learning method based on Laplacian Eigenmaps with incremental novel sample embedding capability. We then explore a wide variety of deterministic and stochastic nonlinear AEs, such as basic, sparse, denoising, and contrastive. Furthermore, the relationship between AEs and manifold learning is discussed. Finally, numerous practical examples are included to highlight the real-life applicability of these networks. The chapter concludes with several computer projects and challenging problems.

title: TFTrack: A Template-Free Framework for Efficient 3D Point Cloud Tracking
abstract: LiDAR-based 3D Single Object Tracking (3D SOT) is critical for robotic perception and navigation and aims to localize dynamic objects across frames in sparse point clouds. Existing methods, rooted in the Siamese tracking paradigm from 2D vision, rely on costly dual-input designs and excessive motion modeling guided by template priors, hindering their efficiency. Our in-depth analysis reveals: (i) the template paradigm is redundant, as the previous bounding box center encodes sufficient historical context; (ii) complex motion modeling is unnecessary, as geometric alignment provides adequate motion priors. Based on the above findings, we propose the first Template-Free Tracking framework (TFTrack). The novel framework eliminates the need for template-search pairings and operates directly on the current frame guided solely by the prior bounding box center and size. We instantiate this paradigm into three variants: TFTrack-Voxel, TFTrack-Pillar, and TFTrack-Point, to explore different 3D representations under a unified framework, ensuring flexibility across sparse and dense scenes. Extensive experiments on KITTI and nuScenes benchmarks show that TFTrack is competitive with leading template-based trackers, while reducing FLOPs by approximately 50% and running at approximately 120 FPS. By simplifying overcomplicated motion-centric designs, TFTrack establishes a new minimalist paradigm for efficient 3D point cloud tracking, paving the way for real-time and resource-efficient deployment in embedded robotic systems, such as autonomous vehicles. The code is available at https://github.com/tftrack-anonymous/TFTrack/tree/main.

title: Propaq: A Python package for Heisenberg Propagation
abstract: We introduce Propaq, a performant and flexible Python package implementing Heisenberg propagation techniques for classically simulating quantum circuits. Propaq is compatible with major quantum software packages like Qiskit and Cirq, and matches or outperforms similar state-of-the-art packages for Heisenberg propagation. Beyond this, Propaq has multiple distinguishing features for simulation and research. These include Heisenberg propagation in any basis, hybrid Schrödinger-Heisenberg simulation, custom truncation and noisy simulation methods, and detailed logging information for analyzing simulation accuracy, runtime, and memory usage. We describe these features, how to use Propaq for research, and its backend implementation.

title: CircuitLens: Reasoning Circuits as Data Selection Signals for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is sensitive to which problems a model trains on, yet existing selection criteria--difficulty filtering, hand-curation, reward-trajectory scoring--assess data value as an intrinsic property of problems, independent of the model that will learn from them. We introduce Circuit Reasoning Score (CRS), a selection signal derived from 46 reasoning-sensitive attention heads identified via contrastive ablation, computed in a single forward pass on the frozen base model without reward labels or rollouts. CRS runs against the intuitive hypothesis that stronger reasoning-circuit engagement produces better training data: on Qwen2.5-Math-7B, the lowest-engagement decile improves over random selection on three medium-difficulty benchmarks (GSM8K +2.0 pp, OlympiadBench +1.6 pp, Minerva +2.9 pp), while the highest-engagement decile gains less and is indistinguishable from the middle decile. The advantage has boundary conditions: on a domain-curated pool no selection method separates from the others; at 1.5B scale the useful direction differs; and the lowest-reward training condition produces the strongest downstream generalization. Within the Qwen2.5-Math settings tested, RLVR data selection appears regime-dependent rather than reducible to a static ranking of problem quality.

title: Federated Neuro-Symbolic Learning for Privacy-Preserving Intelligent Edge Systems
abstract: Intelligent Edge Systems – smart cameras, wearable technology, connected cars and industrial sensors – are creating a growing need to learn from local data at the edge. The two main lines of research that have attempted to address this problem differ. On one hand, Federated Learning (FL) enables training of common models based on the raw data remaining on each device. FL protects user privacy since the model parameters never leave the device. However, FL produces "opaque" (statistical-only) predictors that fail to generalize well in the presence of data heterogeneity and that provide no formal guarantees. On the other hand, Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) learning combines neural perception (e.g., deep neural networks for image classification) with symbolic reasoning, resulting in models that are both efficient with regard to data usage and interpretable, and that are capable of encoding a priori domain knowledge (rules). While NeSy learning has been primarily studied within centralized environments and therefore does not take into consideration the challenges associated with distributed or decentralized learning (such as edge-based intelligent systems), we propose a new paradigm called Federated Neuro-Symbolic Learning (FNSL) for the purpose of enabling NeSy models to be learned in a Federated environment while maintaining formal privacy protection. In our proposed framework, each client (a representative edge system) contains a neural encoder which feeds the encoded information into a differentiable symbolic reasoner. Our server collects masked neural parameter updates from clients and uses this information to refine a collective symbolic knowledge base. To protect users' data and maintain differential privacy during the process of collecting parameter updates, we use secure aggregation methods. Moreover, we adaptively weight domain knowledge according to the confidence assigned to each symbolically represented rule. We demonstrate through experiments using image, sensor and tabular benchmark datasets and non-IID partitioning schemes that FNSL achieves improvements of 4-7 percentage points in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art FL baselines. Additionally, we show that FNSL reduces the amount of uplink communication required per iteration by more than 50%. Lastly, we examine how tightly enforcing privacy budgets impacts performance.

Moreover, we adaptively weight domain knowledge according to the confidence assigned to each symbolically represented rule. We demonstrate through experiments using image, sensor and tabular benchmark datasets and non-IID partitioning schemes that FNSL achieves improvements of 4-7 percentage points in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art FL baselines. title: Adaptive Representation Learning for Streaming Data with Memory Constraints
abstract: This paper presents an adaptive representation learning framework tailored for streaming data environments constrained by limited memory. The core challenge in applying traditional representation learning techniques to continuous data streams lies in the need to retain sufficient information while managing computational resources. Our approach addresses this issue through a dynamically pruning and growing representation, effectively balancing accuracy and efficiency. We introduce a mechanism where a minimal core representation is maintained, and new features are selectively added based on their impact on performance or the evolving data distribution. This adaptive strategy allows the model to continually refine its representation without incurring excessive memory overhead. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, providing a robust solution for representation learning in resource-scarce streaming data scenarios. The key innovations include the dynamic pruning and growing strategy, the feature selection criterion based on performance improvement and distribution adaptation, and the overall architecture designed for efficient memory usage. This work contributes to the field by offering a practical and scalable approach to representation learning for streaming data, addressing a critical limitation in existing methods.

title: 拓扑结构驱动的机器学习模型
abstract: This paper introduces a novel machine learning model leveraging topological structure to dynamically adjust parameters and enhance model generalization. Traditional machine learning often relies on fixed parameter settings, limiting the model's ability to adapt to diverse data. We propose a method where the model's internal structure, represented as a topological graph, guides the optimization process. This approach enables the model to automatically fine-tune its parameters based on the specific characteristics of the input data, resulting in improved performance across a broader range of datasets. The core mechanism involves constructing a topological graph representing the data distribution and using this graph to guide the optimization of model parameters. This allows the model to identify and exploit underlying patterns within the data, leading to more robust and adaptable learning. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in both accuracy and generalization. We believe this approach offers a significant advancement in machine learning, particularly for tasks requiring adaptability and robust performance.

title: Fractal Neural Networks for Hierarchical Feature Extraction
abstract: This paper introduces Fractal Neural Networks (FNNs) as a novel approach to hierarchical feature extraction within deep learning. Traditional neural network architectures, while effective, often struggle to efficiently capture complex, multi-scale hierarchical relationships within data. FNNs address this limitation by employing a fractal-inspired design, utilizing recursive, self-similar layers to create nested representations of the input. The core claim is that this structural approach enables more efficient and effective hierarchical feature learning. The proposed architecture mirrors the branching patterns found in fractals, where each layer operates on a downsampled version of the input, generating increasingly abstract and refined representations. We detail the mathematical formulation and key concepts underpinning FNNs, demonstrating their potential to outperform conventional networks in tasks requiring the extraction of intricate hierarchical features. The presented framework offers a fundamentally different perspective on hierarchical learning, promising improved performance and potentially reducing computational complexity.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Cooperative Reward Shaping
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) presents significant challenges due to the difficulty in designing reward functions that effectively encourage collaboration. Traditional reward structures frequently lead to inefficient learning, as agents may prioritize individual gains over collective success. This paper proposes a novel approach to address this issue: dynamic reward shaping. Our method dynamically adjusts the reward function based on the overall progress of the multi-agent system, providing more immediate and relevant feedback to agents. This mechanism fosters better coordination and ultimately leads to more efficient learning and improved performance in cooperative tasks. We detail the theoretical underpinnings, the algorithm design, and discuss potential applications. The key contributions include a formally defined dynamic reward shaping framework and a corresponding algorithm for its implementation. We demonstrate, through a theoretical analysis and simplified examples, the efficacy of this approach compared to static reward shaping.

title: Time-Travel Quantum Computing Theory
abstract: This paper explores the theoretical implications of time travel within the context of quantum computing. We propose a novel model that leverages quantum superposition and measurement to simulate the influence of past events on present quantum systems. The core claim is that a carefully designed time-traveling quantum computation framework can provide insights into historical phenomena and allow for the simulation of past quantum states, offering a fundamentally new approach to research and modeling. The paper details the model's construction, potential applications, and challenges, ultimately arguing for the necessity of incorporating temporal considerations into quantum computation.

title: Deep Learning-Based Program Formal Verification (DLBFV)
abstract: This paper proposes Deep Learning-Based Program Formal Verification (DLBFV), a novel approach leveraging the power of deep learning to enhance the efficiency and coverage of program formal verification. Traditional program verification techniques often struggle with the complexity and scale of modern software, leading to limitations in both speed and thoroughness. DLBFV addresses this challenge by training a deep learning model to learn semantic information from program code and subsequently utilize this knowledge for automated formal verification. The core claim of DLBFV is that deep learning models can effectively contribute to program formal verification, significantly improving verification efficiency and coverage. This paper details the methodology, exploring the model architecture, training process, and verification strategy employed within DLBFV. We demonstrate the potential of this approach and outline future research directions.

title: Probabilistic Relational Programming with Bayesian Graph Embeddings
abstract: This paper introduces a novel programming paradigm, Probabilistic Relational Programming with Bayesian Graph Embeddings (PRP-GBE), designed to address the challenges of representing and reasoning with complex relational knowledge. The core problem lies in the "curse of dimensionality" inherent in traditional probabilistic models when dealing with intricate relational structures. Our approach combines Relational Programming, which provides a natural way to express relationships between entities, with Bayesian Graph Embeddings, which learn compact, low-dimensional representations of these graphs. Nodes in the graph represent entities and are associated with continuous probability distributions, while edges represent relations also parameterized by these distributions. The Bayesian graph embeddings effectively learn a latent space that significantly reduces the computational complexity of probabilistic inference and learning tasks. This integration allows for direct probabilistic reasoning within relational data structures, offering a potentially powerful solution for knowledge representation, reasoning, and ultimately, more robust and adaptable AI systems. We present a foundational framework for PRP-GBE, detailing the core components and outlining potential applications.

title: Adaptive Optimization of Quantum Algorithms
abstract: Quantum algorithms, renowned for their potential to solve complex problems beyond the capabilities of classical computers, often exhibit inherent sensitivity to initial conditions and parameter choices. This sensitivity can significantly impact algorithm performance, hindering their ability to achieve optimal solutions. This paper proposes a novel adaptive optimization method specifically designed for quantum algorithms, focusing on dynamically adjusting algorithm parameters based on runtime analysis. We introduce a framework that leverages quantum algorithm properties to automatically refine parameter settings, thereby maximizing efficiency and exploring a broader range of solution spaces. This approach aims to surpass the limitations of traditional optimization techniques by proactively addressing the unique challenges posed by quantum computation.

title: 基于拓扑的非线性矩阵的自适应学习
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to matrix optimization utilizing a dynamically adjusted topology. We propose a self-adaptive learning algorithm that leverages the inherent non-linear properties of matrix operations to optimize complex matrices. The core mechanism centers around constructing a dynamic topology that responds to the matrix's state, allowing the system to adjust its behavior in real-time. This approach offers a promising path towards intelligent system design, addressing limitations of traditional optimization methods. The paper details the algorithm's design, its mathematical framework, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in a simplified, yet illustrative, scenario.

title: Quantum Machine Learning Algorithm Design and Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the design and optimization of algorithms within the burgeoning field of quantum machine learning (QML). The core aim is to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of QML techniques by proposing novel algorithmic approaches and implementing effective optimization strategies. We investigate various methods, including quantum support vector machines (QSVMs), quantum principal component analysis (QPCA), and quantum neural networks (QNNs), focusing on how to leverage quantum properties such as superposition and entanglement to accelerate learning processes and potentially surpass the limitations of classical algorithms. The optimization strategies discussed encompass both algorithmic refinements and the selection of appropriate quantum hardware architectures. The results presented demonstrate the potential of tailored QML algorithms to achieve significant improvements in specific machine learning tasks. Further research is needed to fully realize the transformative capabilities of QML, but this work provides a foundational understanding and a roadmap for future development.

title: The Hidden Frame: How Large Language Models Impact Democratic Society
abstract: Large language models are rapidly becoming an interface between citizens and political information. They are often regarded as "a better Google." While this analogy might work for some instances, it is unintuitively problematic for democratic politics. A search engine retrieves human-authored documents, while a language model generates novel text that necessarily embeds invisible framing decisions. Because conveying knowledge involves framing, a system that generates answers cannot serve as a neutral conduit to "all human knowledge." Instead, these systems are becoming a new kind of political intermediary. Mechanistic evidence shows that partisan identity is encoded as a locatable geometric direction inside the Llama 3.1 8B model, and that alignment training masks rather than removes this structure. Building on that evidence, we use the model's training cutoff in 2023 to make those frames visible. This cutpoint auspiciously falls just before a dramatic realignment in American politics marked by the second Trump administration and the MAHA transformation of health politics, providing us with a natural experiment. We find that the model presents temporally contingent partisan alignments as {\em knowledge}, with no reliable mechanism for distinguishing fact from opinion. Because citizens judge political claims by who made them and when, an answer that carries neither cue hampers the judgment on which self-governance depends. Large language models purporting to summarize "all human knowledge" are, in actuality, simply magnifying the cultural and partisan divides inherent in their training data.

title: Masking Radar Cognition under Adversarial Surveillance: A Distributional Privacy Framework
abstract: In this article, we propose an online electronic counter-countermeasure (ECCM) framework designed to conceal the strategic decision-making processes of a cognitive radar (CR) operating under adversarial surveillance. We model the CR under two distinct decision paradigms: a static constrained utility-maximizing behavior and a dynamic expected utility-maximizing behavior. The radar's utility function is modeled via a von Mises--Fisher (vMF) distribution, with the distributional parameter constituting the private information to be protected from adversarial inference. We adopt a distribution privacy framework to conceal this private information and provide formal distribution privacy guarantees for cognition masking. In this work, we develop cognition-hiding algorithms for both static constrained utility maximization (WDPCH-SU), and dynamic expected utility maximization (WDPCH-DU). Through rigorous mathematical analysis, we show that both WDPCH-SU and WDPCH-DU satisfy $ε$-distribution privacy ($ε$-DistP) against inference-based adversarial attacks and present the privacy--performance trade-off bounds, quantifying utility loss (in static setting) and expected utility deviation (in dynamic setting) as functions of $ε$. Numerical results show that WDPCH-SU gives about 15\% improvement in utility loss at maximum privacy compared to the existing methodology while WDPCH-DU achieves a greater reduction in adversarial Fisher information without requiring explicit Fisher information constraints, at a moderate, analytically bounded utility deviation. These results are highly promising in many 6G communication scenarios such as network slicing for automated driving and swarm UAV coordination, where it is essential to keep the resource allocation policy robust against privacy attacks.

title: Spectral Criterion for Disorder-Free Localization of Quantum Walks on Hypercube: QBN Approach
abstract: We study disorder-free localization in a spin-coupled quantum walk on the hypercube within the quantum Bernoulli noises framework. We derive a general criterion for disorder-free localization: it occurs if and only if some spectral subspace of a reduced unitary evolution contains a vector whose position marginal probability is non-uniform. For the Grover walk with distance-dependent coupling \(ϕ_σ=|σ|π/(n+1)\) in dimension \(d=4\), we explicitly construct a non-uniform fixed point in the all \(+1\) spin configuration. This implies that disorder-free localization occurs in our model.

title: EEG-Driven Decoding Framework for Passenger Hazard Perception in Highly Automated Vehicles
abstract: Reliable risk assessment remains a central challenge for Autonomous Vehicles (AVs). Despite advances in automation, passenger cognition provides a non-intrusive auxiliary signal that improves both objective and perceived safety without requiring active human intervention. We introduce an Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) that decodes passenger neural responses for both Risk Prediction (RP) and Danger Identification (DI), explicitly modeling humans as passengers to match real-world AV use. To achieve this, we propose the Passenger Cognitive Model (PCM), Risk-aware Sequential Labeling (RSL), and the Passenger EEG Decoding Strategy (PEDS), which integrates a 3D Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (3D-CRNN) model for joint EEG decoding. Experimental results show that 3D-CRNN achieves a Balanced Accuracy (BA) of $95.3\% \pm 2.7\%$ in RP and improves single-subject DI from $80.9\% \pm 3.9\%$ to $85.0\% \pm 3.2\%$ with RSL. Event-wise analyses further show that 3D-CRNN consistently outperforms other models across different event types in RP and DI. In generalization experiments, 3D-CRNN achieves $77.0\% \pm 5.3\%$ BA in cross-session DI and $77.4\% \pm 1.1\%$ BA on seen subjects in cross-subject evaluation, while maintaining a $64.9\% \pm 8.5\%$ BA on unseen subjects, demonstrating promising generalizability and transferability across both intra-subject and inter-subject variability. These findings establish an Electroencephalogram (EEG) decoding framework for AV passenger hazard perception and suggest that passenger cognitive signals can provide auxiliary supervision for future AV decision-making and Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF) support.

title: Exponentiated gradients support effective learning in biologically relevant scenarios
abstract: Keynote address. Computational neuroscience relies on gradient descent (GD) for training artificial neural network (ANN) models of the brain. The advantage of GD is that it is effective at learning difficult tasks. However, it produces ANNs that are a poor phenomenological fit to biology, making them less relevant as models of the brain. Specifically, it violates Dale's law, by allowing synapses to change from excitatory to inhibitory, and leads to synaptic weights that are not log-normally distributed, contradicting experimental data. Here, starting from first principles of optimization theory, I will present an alternative learning algorithm, exponentiated gradient (EG), that respects Dale's Law and produces log-normal weights, without losing the power of learning with gradients. We show that in biologically relevant settings EG outperforms GD, including learning from sparsely relevant signals and dealing with synaptic pruning. Altogether, our results show that EG is a superior learning algorithm for modelling the brain with ANNs.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks via Internal Feedback Loops
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to training neural networks – Self-Correcting Neural Networks (SCNNs) – designed to mitigate the challenges of drifting gradients and inaccurate representations often encountered during extended training. The core concept involves integrating internal feedback loops within the network architecture. These loops continuously monitor the output of specific layers and, leveraging a learned error signal, dynamically adjust the weights to correct deviations from desired behavior. This creates a self-correcting mechanism, fostering greater stability and robustness. The theoretical framework details the mathematical formulation of the correction process, highlighting the role of the error signal and the iterative weight adjustment. The proposed SCNN architecture offers a promising pathway towards more reliable and efficient neural network training, particularly for complex tasks and long training durations. The key contribution lies in providing a demonstrable method for inherent self-correction, addressing a significant limitation of traditional neural network training methodologies. ---

title: Title: Adaptive Geometry Transformation Quantum State Analysis
abstract: This paper investigates the impact of adaptive geometry transformations on quantum states, proposing a novel quantum state analysis method to understand quantum state evolution and stability. We explore the potential of utilizing adaptive algorithms to dynamically adjust quantum state characteristics during transformation, offering a fundamentally different approach to quantum state analysis. The core claim is that this approach could reveal new quantum state patterns and dynamics.

title: 基于量子密钥分发协议的密码学体系
abstract: This paper introduces a novel cryptographic system based on Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) principles. Traditional cryptographic methods are vulnerable to attacks from both classical and quantum computers. This research explores the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement and key distribution to establish a fundamentally secure communication channel. We propose a QKD-based system leveraging quantum entanglement for secure key exchange and decryption, analyzing its security properties and potential advantages over existing cryptographic techniques. The core claim focuses on the enhanced security afforded by quantum mechanics, specifically the vulnerability of classical encryption to attacks leveraging the inherent properties of entangled states. The paper details the design of the QKD protocol, its security analysis, and potential applications within a secure communication framework.

title: 自适应机器学习的领域知识嵌入
abstract: This paper explores the application of adaptive machine learning to incorporate domain knowledge into model representations. Traditional machine learning models often struggle to effectively leverage domain knowledge, limiting their performance and interpretability. This work proposes a novel framework that dynamically embeds domain knowledge into the model during training, improving generalization and providing enhanced explainability. We detail the core mechanisms behind this approach, including a modular architecture and iterative refinement strategies, and demonstrate its effectiveness through a series of simulated and experimental studies. The core claim is that this framework significantly enhances model performance and interpretability, addressing the limitations of traditional approaches.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning for Robotics
abstract: Quantum-enhanced reinforcement learning (QEL) offers the potential to significantly improve the performance of robotic systems, particularly in navigating complex environments and adapting to dynamic situations. This paper explores the integration of quantum computing with reinforcement learning to accelerate learning, enhance exploration, and improve adaptation. We propose a novel approach that leverages quantum annealing and quantum reinforcement learning to overcome the limitations of classical RL in challenging scenarios. The core claim is that combining these two paradigms will lead to enhanced robot navigation and control capabilities. The study focuses on demonstrating the effectiveness of this combined approach through simulations and preliminary results.

title: Quantum-Inspired Entropy Maximization for Feature Selection
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to feature selection leveraging quantum-inspired optimization, specifically quantum annealing, to maximize entropy within a candidate feature subset. Traditional feature selection techniques often face challenges in high-dimensional datasets, struggling to pinpoint the most impactful features. Our method addresses this by framing feature selection as an entropy maximization problem. The core idea is to employ a quantum annealing algorithm to explore the feature space, iteratively refining the subset until the entropy reaches a maximum value. This approach aims to identify features that contribute significantly to the information content related to the target variable. We demonstrate the potential of this approach compared to conventional methods, highlighting its ability to effectively handle complex datasets and improve model performance. The theoretical framework is presented, along with a detailed explanation of the algorithm and its underlying principles. The results, while not based on empirical experimentation due to the nature of the theoretical exploration, provide a strong argument for the viability and potential advantages of quantum-inspired techniques in feature selection.

title: Nonlinear Quantum Entanglement Simulation Framework (NQEF)
abstract: This paper introduces the NQEF, a novel framework for simulating non-linear quantum entanglement. Traditional quantum simulation methods often struggle with complex entanglement scenarios, limiting their applicability to specific quantum systems. The NQEF addresses this limitation through the implementation of a "纠缠状态映射" algorithm, which dynamically transforms quantum entanglement states into corresponding quantum circuits, facilitating a more accurate and general simulation of entanglement evolution. We present a novel approach utilizing quantum machine learning to improve the fidelity and interpretability of the simulation. The NQEF offers a robust and versatile tool for exploring and understanding quantum information and quantum computation, paving the way for advancements in quantum algorithm design and verification.

title: Probability Association Matrix Dynamic Adjustment Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic probability association matrix algorithm designed to optimize the training of machine learning models through real-time parameter adjustment. Traditional parameter adjustment methods are typically static and fail to adapt effectively to evolving data distributions and training dynamics. This algorithm leverages the concept of probability association matrices to dynamically adjust the matrix weights based on model predictions and data, offering a more efficient and robust approach. The core mechanism centers on continuous learning and error-based weight adjustment, enabling the algorithm to maintain optimal model performance and generalization capabilities. This work addresses a critical limitation in traditional machine learning, providing a practical framework for real-time parameter tuning.

title: Adaptive Neuron Growth Networks
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Neuron Growth Networks (ANGNs), a novel neural network architecture designed for dynamic adaptation to varying input complexities and network performance. ANGNs utilize a reinforcement learning-based mechanism where individual neurons dynamically adjust their parameters – both synaptic weights and intrinsic neuron properties – based on their output error and the overall state of the network. Unlike traditional adaptive learning approaches that primarily focus on parameter tuning, ANGNS introduce a core mechanism for self-organization and structural modification, enabling the network to grow or prune neurons and connections proportionally to the complexity of the input data and the efficiency of the network's operation. The key innovation lies in the integration of reinforcement learning with a network growth/pruning strategy, allowing for a truly adaptive and scalable neural network architecture. The theoretical framework and the proposed algorithm are presented, demonstrating the potential of ANGNS for tasks requiring adaptability and robustness.

title: Quantum Field Theory-Based Computational Complexity Research
abstract: This research investigates computational complexity problems through the lens of quantum field theory (QFT). Traditional approaches to complexity theory often rely on algorithmic and logical arguments, while QFT provides a powerful framework for analyzing systems with high dimensionality and entanglement. This paper explores how QFT concepts – such as renormalization, path integrals, and the representation of states as quantum fields – can be applied to understand and potentially mitigate the challenges inherent in certain computational problems. Specifically, we examine how the inherent probabilistic nature of QFT, combined with its ability to handle complex, high-dimensional spaces, might offer new perspectives on problems like NP-completeness and the limits of computation. We propose a framework for translating complexity problems into QFT-inspired models and discuss potential avenues for leveraging these models to explore the landscape of computational complexity. The core contribution of this work lies in establishing a novel methodology for tackling complexity questions by drawing upon the established tools and techniques of QFT. We investigate the potential for utilizing QFT's inherent parallelism and its ability to represent exponentially large state spaces to overcome limitations faced by classical algorithms.

title: MI-PEFT: Mixture-of-Experts Integrated Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Protein Language Models Improves Acidophilic Proteins Classification
abstract: Acidophilic proteins that remain stable and functional under highly acidic conditions, are important for industrial biocatalysis, acid-related bioprocessing, and the discovery of acid-stable enzymes. However, their identification relies heavily on time-consuming experimental screening methods. With the rapid growth of protein sequence databases, the need for computational identification methods that are both accurate and efficient has become stronger. The emergence of protein language models (PLMs) has significantly improved the sequence representation of downstream biological prediction tasks. This paper proposes MI-PEFT, a mixture-of-experts integrated parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework. Built on the ESM C-600M backbone, the framework incorporates LoRA-based PEFT methods and a DeepSeekMoE-based classification head to resolve the limitations of PEFT and significantly improve computational efficiency. Notably, this task is characterized by a significant class imbalance in the dataset, making high specificity particularly challenging. The experimental results demonstrate that MI-PEFT on PLMs, especially {\text{C}}^{\text{3}}\text{A}, serves as an efficient tool for identifying acidophilic proteins and a constrained pathway that helps resolve class-imbalance by preserving the pretrained representations.

title: TV-SGS: Gaussian Splatting with Geometric Information Propagation via Tensor Voting under sparse views
abstract: Gaussian Splatting has been effective in inferring scene representations that excel in novel view synthesis. Multiple splats cooperate seamlessly to synthesize the pixels of novel views and are jointly optimized even though they only affect each other indirectly, via pixels they project to in common. We present an approach that enables direct communication among splats to enhance the geometric structures they form in 3D. This is accomplished by Tensor Voting, which was originally designed to infer structures from noisy inputs and has been adapted here to provide supervision during test-time optimization, leading to more accurate scene geometry. We introduce a new class of 3D losses that do not rely on rendering and can be combined with essentially all losses previously reported in the literature. Our 3D losses are especially effective when the input views are sparse and geometric regularization is essential due to limited supervision from the images. Our method is easy to integrate with a diverse set of backbones, and our experiments on the DTU and Tanks-and-Temples datasets demonstrate that TV-SGS improves the geometry of the outputs compared to the backbone, while maintaining or improving rendering quality.

title: Unified Vision-Centric Pedestrian Crossing Action Prediction via Adaptive Patch Projection and Proactive Spatial Rectification
abstract: Vision cues are available and informative for pedestrian action prediction, but obtaining stable target-centric representations from video frames remains challenging without frame-level external perception cues. Thus, most methods rely on additional perception modules or multi-source information fusion, leaving the reliability of vision-centric setting an open question. To this end, we propose ViCross, a vision-centric pedestrian crossing action prediction framework powered by multimodal large language models, which maintains target-centric reasoning from video frames without additional perception modules beyond first-frame target initialization. While multimodal large language models exhibit strong visual understanding, applying them directly to vision-centric action prediction faces two challenges. First, accurately perceiving target pedestrians often requires high resolution inputs and dense visual tokenization, making full-frame encoding computationally prohibitive. ViCross tackles this with Variable Resolution Patch Mapping module for efficient token allocation while preserving key pedestrian details. Second, missing spatiotemporal priors hinder consistent cross frame reasoning. ViCross mitigates this with a Spatial Constraint Enhancement Strategy that captures past motion, future locations, and action semantics for training-time proactive spatial rectification. Extensive experiments show that ViCross delivers clear gains in vision-centric prediction settings and is competitive with multi-source fusion approaches in several settings. Code is available at https://github.com/2tianyao1/ViCross.git.

title: External Difference Families Arising from Two or Three Cyclotomic Classes
abstract: We study external difference families arising from cyclotomic classes in finite fields from the viewpoint of a fixed number of blocks. For families consisting of even-indexed cyclotomic classes, the EDF condition can be expressed in terms of relations among cyclotomic numbers. We first study the two-block case and recover a classical characterization in terms of quadratic forms. Our main result shows that, for a prime $p=12k+1$, the family $\{C_0^6,C_2^6,C_4^6\}$ forms an EDF in $\mathbb{F}_p$ if and only if $k$ is a square. The proofs combine symmetry relations of cyclotomic numbers with their explicit evaluations.

title: Adaptive Quantum Tunneling for Signal Reconstruction in Non-Linear Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive quantum tunneling to signal reconstruction in non-linear systems. Traditional signal reconstruction methods often fall short when dealing with complex, non-linear data due to the limitations of fixed probability distributions. We propose a novel quantum tunneling algorithm that dynamically adjusts the tunneling probability based on the observed signal, thereby enhancing reconstruction accuracy. The core mechanism leverages quantum fluctuations to achieve this dynamic adjustment. This approach offers a potentially transformative method for signal reconstruction in challenging scenarios, addressing limitations inherent in classical approaches.

title: Adaptive Formal Verification of Programs
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program generation that leverages adaptive formal verification. The core idea is to integrate a formal verification engine into a program generation loop, creating a feedback mechanism where verification results guide and refine the generated code. Unlike traditional approaches that treat formal verification as a post-generation validation step, this work positions it as an active component within the generation process. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this adaptive approach, focusing on the construction of a robust verification engine and generator interaction. The method allows for the automatic construction of programs that demonstrably satisfy specified properties, thereby improving software reliability and reducing the need for extensive manual debugging. We demonstrate the feasibility of this concept through a theoretical framework and outline potential future research directions.

title: Dynamic Controlled Quantum Resource Allocation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum resource allocation that addresses the inherent challenges posed by quantum decoherence. Traditional quantum computing resource management strategies often rely on static allocation schemes, which are ill-suited for the dynamic nature of quantum systems. This research proposes a dynamic control framework that leverages real-time monitoring of quantum state decoherence to optimize resource allocation. The core claim is that by continuously adapting to the fluctuating decoherence levels, we can maximize the effectiveness of quantum computations. The proposed mechanism involves measuring decoherence, evaluating current task resource needs, and dynamically adjusting qubit allocation, control, and error correction protocols. This approach offers a significant advancement over existing methods and provides a pathway toward more robust and efficient quantum computation. The system aims to mitigate the detrimental effects of decoherence, a primary obstacle in the practical realization of quantum algorithms. The theoretical framework and the proposed control strategies are detailed within this document.

title: Self-Adapting Quantum Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm, termed "Self-Adapting Quantum Algorithms" (SAQA), designed to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of quantum computations. Traditional quantum algorithms often rely on fixed, pre-defined procedures, presenting limitations in their adaptability and performance. SAQA leverages the unique characteristics of self-adaptive quantum algorithms to dynamically adjust parameters and quantum states, enabling a more flexible and robust approach to problem-solving. We explore the core mechanism behind this adaptation, detailing how the algorithm iteratively refines its quantum state to optimize performance based on the input data and the algorithm's progress. The paper presents a theoretical framework and initial experimental results demonstrating the potential of SAQA to outperform conventional algorithms in specific, carefully selected scenarios. The core claim of this work is that SAQA offers a significant improvement in efficiency and accuracy through adaptive parameter adjustments.

title: Title: Bayesian Parameter Allocation with Adaptive Noise Distribution (BAPD)
abstract: This paper presents Bayesian Parameter Allocation with Adaptive Noise Distribution (BAPD), a novel algorithm for parameter optimization that addresses the challenge of efficiently managing uncertainty during the allocation of parameters in complex systems. Traditional Bayesian methods often rely on fixed noise distributions, leading to suboptimal performance and computational cost, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional parameter spaces. BAPD dynamically adjusts the noise variance based on observed uncertainty, optimizing both accuracy and computational efficiency across a wide range of parameter spaces. The core mechanism involves a dynamically updating Bayesian updating scheme that leverages a novel approach to uncertainty quantification. This paper explores the design and implementation of BAPD, demonstrating its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results across several benchmark datasets. We highlight the algorithm's ability to effectively mitigate the challenges associated with parameter optimization, offering a significant advancement in the field of Bayesian inference.

title: Adaptive Kernel Learning via Meta-Gradient Descent
abstract: Kernel learning methods have demonstrated remarkable success in various machine learning tasks, particularly in scenarios where explicit feature engineering is challenging. However, a significant bottleneck lies in the need for manual kernel selection and meticulous parameter tuning, a process often hampered by subjective choices and lacking theoretical guarantees. This paper proposes a novel adaptive kernel learning framework leveraging meta-learning and gradient descent. The core idea is to treat kernel parameter optimization as a meta-learning problem, where the kernel parameters themselves are learned via gradient descent on a meta-objective function. This function quantifies the performance of the learned kernel across a set of related tasks. The system dynamically adapts the kernel, aiming to maximize its predictive accuracy across a diverse range of datasets. Our approach automates the often-difficult task of kernel selection and parameter tuning, offering a more robust and efficient solution compared to traditional methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through theoretical analysis and conceptual discussions, outlining the key components and potential improvements. ---

title: 基于动态拓扑的自适应机器学习的生物进化算法
abstract: This paper explores the application of dynamic topology as a foundational element in an adaptive machine learning framework for biological evolution. Traditional evolutionary algorithms often focus on static individual changes, limiting the scope of evolutionary processes. This research proposes a novel approach that leverages dynamic topology – a mathematical framework describing the connectedness and branching of networks – to constrain mutation and adaptation, providing a more robust and potentially efficient simulation of biological evolution. We introduce a framework that dynamically modifies the topology of the evolutionary landscape, influencing gene mutation rates and adaptation pathways. The core mechanism centers around the concept of 'topology-driven evolution,' where the underlying network structure dictates the evolutionary trajectory. The paper details the implementation of this framework, provides a preliminary analysis of its performance, and discusses future research directions.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Accelerated Symbolic Reasoning
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement to significantly accelerate symbolic reasoning and knowledge graph queries. Traditional symbolic reasoning methods often struggle with the inherent challenges of encoding and searching large amounts of logical information, leading to computational bottlenecks. We propose a novel approach that utilizes quantum entanglement to overcome these limitations. The core idea is to decompose symbolic logic problems into multiple entangled qubit sets. Through superposition and interference of these entangled states, parallel inference is enabled. Finally, quantum measurements yield the solution. This approach promises exponential speedups compared to classical methods, offering a fundamentally new paradigm for logical deduction and knowledge retrieval. The paper details the theoretical framework, outlining the key equations and mathematical representations underpinning the proposed methodology. We present a detailed model that incorporates the principles of quantum mechanics to accelerate the process of symbolic inference. This research contributes to the emerging field of quantum information science and its potential applications in artificial intelligence and knowledge management.

title: Algorithmic Auditing of Machine Learning Models using Differential Privacy
abstract: The increasing deployment of machine learning (ML) models across diverse sectors raises significant concerns regarding bias, fairness, and potential vulnerabilities. Traditional auditing methods often require access to raw, sensitive data, directly contradicting data privacy regulations and potentially exacerbating existing biases. This paper introduces a novel algorithmic auditing framework leveraging differential privacy (DP) to assess ML model behavior without exposing underlying data. The core concept involves generating perturbed model outputs and analyzing their statistical distribution to detect anomalies indicative of bias or vulnerabilities. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach, highlighting its ability to provide privacy-preserving insights into model performance while mitigating the risks associated with conventional auditing techniques. The proposed framework offers a practical solution for improving model governance and promoting responsible AI development.

title: Relational Reinforcement Learning with Fractal State Spaces
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to reinforcement learning (RL) that utilizes fractal geometry to represent state spaces, particularly beneficial in complex relational environments. Traditional RL agents often struggle with environments where relationships between elements are crucial for optimal decision-making. Our core claim is that representing states as fractal-like structures, which inherently capture hierarchical dependencies, significantly improves an agent's ability to learn and perform. The mechanism involves an agent learning to navigate this fractal state space, leading to efficient exploration and exploitation of intricate relational patterns. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework, highlighting its potential advantages over conventional state representation techniques. The key innovation lies in the efficient encoding of relational data through a fractal structure, leading to a more expressive and navigable state space. This approach addresses the limitations of standard RL in scenarios demanding a nuanced understanding of interconnected elements. The overall goal is to create RL agents capable of mastering complex relational tasks with improved sample efficiency and generalization capabilities.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Vector Space Interpolation for Deep Learning
abstract: The vanishing gradient problem is a pervasive challenge in deep learning, hindering the effective training of complex models. Traditional methods often struggle to navigate high-dimensional spaces effectively, limiting the ability to capture intricate relationships within the data. This paper proposes a novel method for interpolating between data points in deep learning spaces utilizing a non-Euclidean vector space, leveraging tensor-based projection to improve gradient flow and potentially mitigate the vanishing gradient problem. We introduce a new technique that maps data points to this space, offering a potential solution to this longstanding challenge. The core mechanism centers around a tensor-based projection, which dynamically adjusts the dimensionality of the data representation to optimize gradient propagation. We detail the methodology, provide a comprehensive analysis of its performance, and discuss its implications for deep learning architectures. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential benefits and limitations of this approach.

title: Multi-Year Assessment of Agreement Between Rooftop Photovoltaic Design Estimates and Monitored Performance Data: Sustainable Energy Planning in South-Eastern Poland
abstract: Reliable rooftop photovoltaic planning requires design-stage energy predictions to be verified against actual system performance. The novelty of this study is the integration of a multi-year assessment of agreement with PV*SOL design estimates with an independent assessment of normalized productivity, interannual variability, seasonality, and meteorological effects for several rooftop systems operating under the same regional conditions. PV*SOL, a commercial photovoltaic simulation software used to estimate system energy production during the design stage, was evaluated using three years (2023–2025) of monitored data from three rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems (17.60–75.40 kWp) in Rzeszów, south-eastern Poland. The analysis comprised 108 installation-month observations and included final yield, capacity factor, annual prediction errors, seasonal variability, Pearson correlations, and hierarchical regression. Mean annual final yield ranged from 907.4 to 966.2 kWh/kWp, while annual deviations from PV*SOL design estimates ranged from −0.80% to +7.41%. Monthly final yield was strongly associated with solar irradiation, and the final hierarchical regression model explained 96.4% of its variability. The results indicate that PV*SOL provides a useful annual design reference, but operational monitoring and local benchmark data remain essential for reliable performance assessment. The study supports United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) by improving the evidence base for rooftop photovoltaic planning and monitoring.
